title: Transfer pricing basics for cross-border transaction disputes
p1: A company can sell the same product across borders and still face a tax dispute over the price. Sounds strange? The reason is transfer pricing — a concept that quietly affects many global businesses.
p2: Many people think companies can simply choose any price for transactions between related entities. The reality is different. Tax authorities check whether the price matches what independent businesses would normally charge, because pricing can affect where profits and taxes are reported.
p3: Transfer pricing disputes often happen when two countries disagree on the right price for a cross-border transaction. For example, a parent company selling services to its overseas subsidiary may need to prove that the price is fair and supported by evidence. The key takeaway: good documentation and a clear pricing method can prevent costly conflicts.
conclusion: If a business operates in multiple countries, do you think tax authorities should have more power to review internal company pricing decisions?
